clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant haploinsufficiency of NFKB1 is among the most frequently identified monogenic causes of a common variable immunodeficiency phenotype in adults.
The presentation combines antibody deficiency (recurrent sinopulmonary infection, hypogammaglobulinaemia, reduced switched memory B cells) with prominent autoimmunity and autoinflammation.
Penetrance and expressivity are highly variable, with asymptomatic carriers and severely affected relatives occurring within a single family.
Autoinflammatory or Behcet-like features such as oral and genital ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune cytopenias are characteristic.
There is an increased risk of lymphoid and other malignancy.
Epstein-Barr virus-driven complications and lymphoproliferation may occur.
Immunoglobulin replacement together with targeted management of autoimmune and inflammatory manifestations is the mainstay of care.
reference.pathophysiology: NFKB1 encodes p105, the precursor that is processed to the p50 subunit of the canonical NF-κB transcription factor complex. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants cause haploinsufficiency, reducing availability of p50 and p105 and impairing canonical NF-κB signalling downstream of numerous immune receptors. This disturbs B-cell maturation and antibody production, accounting for the common variable immunodeficiency-like antibody defect, while simultaneously dysregulating inflammatory and tolerance pathways, producing the combined picture of immunodeficiency, autoimmunity and autoinflammation. The wide variation in penetrance and severity reflects the contribution of modifier genes and environmental factors, so that identical variants can be silent in some family members and severe in others.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable immunodeficiency of undefined genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulin quantification (IgG, IgA and IgM)
Specific antibody and vaccine response testing
B-cell subset analysis focusing on switched memory B cells
Genetic sequencing of NFKB1 and broader common variable immunodeficiency gene panels
Autoantibody screen with direct antiglobulin test and blood film for cytopenias
Cross-sectional imaging for lymphoproliferation and bronchiectasis
Malignancy surveillance guided by clinical features
redFlags: Recurrent severe or opportunistic infection with hypogammaglobulinaemia
Antibody deficiency combined with autoimmune cytopenia or inflammatory bowel disease
New lymphadenopathy or constitutional symptoms suggesting lymphoma
Family history of common variable immunodeficiency or autoimmunity with markedly variable severity
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and depends on infection control with immunoglobulin replacement and on autoimmune, inflammatory and malignant complications. These complications, rather than infection alone, are the major sources of morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Confusing NFKB1 (p50/p105, canonical pathway) with NFKB2 (p52/p100, non-canonical pathway), the latter being associated with anterior pituitary and adrenocorticotrophic hormone deficiency.
Interpreting a normal or borderline immunoglobulin level early in disease as excluding the diagnosis, since overt hypogammaglobulinaemia may develop later.
Dismissing the diagnosis because asymptomatic mutation carriers exist within the family.
Misattributing autoinflammatory features to primary Behcet disease.
